java.title: Hello, output
java.intro:
Every Java program starts in `main`. In Basecamp you only see the lines **inside** `main`;
LogicQuest wraps them in `public class Main { public static void main(String[] args) { ... } }` for you.

`System.out.println(x)` prints `x` and then moves to a new line. `System.out.print(x)` stays on the same line.
Every statement ends with a semicolon `;`.

exercises.prompt: What does this print?
exercises.code:
System.out.println("Hello");
System.out.println("World");
exercises.why: Each `println` ends its line, so the words land on two lines.

exercises.prompt: What does this print?
exercises.why: `print` doesn't add a newline, so the three pieces join into one word.

exercises.prompt: Which line prints `Hi` and moves to the next line?
exercises.why: `println` = print + line break. `print` keeps the cursor on the same line.

exercises.prompt: Make it print `5 apples` on one line.
exercises.code:
System.out.___("5 ");
System.out.println("apples");
exercises.why: `print` keeps `5 ` and `apples` on the same line.

exercises.prompt: What does this print?
exercises.code:
System.out.println("2 + 3");
System.out.println(2 + 3);
exercises.why: Inside quotes it's text and printed as-is. Without quotes Java does the maths first.

exercises.prompt: This should print `Ready` but doesn't compile. Fix it.
exercises.code: System.out.println("Ready")
exercises.solution: System.out.println("Ready");
exercises.why: Every Java statement ends with `;`. The compiler error says `';' expected`.

java.title: Variables and types

exercises.prompt: What does this print?
exercises.why: `x = x + 5` reads the old value (10), adds 5, and stores 15 back in `x`.

exercises.prompt: Which type should hold the value `3.75`?
exercises.why: Decimals need `double`. Putting 3.75 in an `int` won't even compile.

exercises.prompt: What does this print?
exercises.why: `+` joins Strings. Spaces only appear where you add them.

exercises.prompt: Declare a `boolean` called `done` set to true.
exercises.code:
___ done = ___;
System.out.println(done);
exercises.why: `boolean` holds exactly `true` or `false`, written in lowercase.

exercises.prompt: Arrange the lines so the program prints `20`.
exercises.why: A variable must be declared before it is used, so declarations come first.

exercises.prompt: Swap the values so it prints `2 1`.
exercises.why: After `a = b`, the old value of `a` is gone. Keep it in a `temp` variable first.

java.title: Operators
java.intro:
`+ - * /` work as you'd expect, with one catch: **int / int gives an int**. `7 / 2` is `3`, the decimal part is dropped.
`%` gives the remainder: `7 % 2` is `1`.

`x += 3` is short for `x = x + 3`, and `x++` adds 1.

exercises.prompt: What does this print?
exercises.why: Two ints → integer division (3). One double makes the result a double (3.5).

exercises.prompt: What does this print?
What is `2 + 3 * 4` in Java?
exercises.why: `*` happens before `+`, just like in maths: 3 × 4 = 12, then 2 + 12.

exercises.prompt: What does this print?
exercises.code:
System.out.println(-7 % 2);
System.out.println(-7 / 2);
exercises.why: Java keeps the sign of the left number for `%` and drops the decimals for `/`, so you get -1 and -3.

exercises.prompt: Print the last digit of `n`.
exercises.code:
int n = 1234;
System.out.println(n ___ 10);
exercises.why: The remainder after dividing by 10 is always the last digit.

exercises.prompt: This should print the average `2.5`, but prints `2.0`. Fix the calculation.
exercises.why: `(a + b) / 2` is int / int = 2 before it is stored. Dividing by `2.0` makes it a decimal division.

java.title: Strings and chars
java.intro:
A `String` is text; a `char` is one character in single quotes, like `'a'`.

- `s.length()` → number of characters
- `s.charAt(i)` → the character at index `i` (starting from 0)
- Compare text with `a.equals(b)`, never `==`.
- A `char` is a number underneath: `'b' - 'a'` is `1`.

exercises.prompt: What does this print?
exercises.why: Indexes run from 0 to length − 1, so the last character is at `length() - 1`.

exercises.prompt: What does this print?
exercises.why: `'a' + 1` is the number 98. Casting back to `char` turns it into `'b'`.

exercises.prompt: How do you check if String `a` has the same text as String `b`?
exercises.why: `==` checks if they are the same object in memory. `.equals` compares the characters.

exercises.prompt: Print every character of `word` on its own line.
exercises.why: `length()` gives the count; `charAt(i)` reads one character.

exercises.prompt: What does this print?
exercises.why: Adding a char to a String appends it. Then `+ 3` turns the length into text too.

exercises.prompt: Print the first and last character of the word you read, separated by a space. For `logic` print `l c`.
exercises.why: First is `charAt(0)`, last is `charAt(w.length() - 1)`.

java.title: Reading input
java.intro:
`Scanner` reads what the user types (stdin):

```java
Scanner sc = new Scanner(System.in);
int n = sc.nextInt();      // next whole number
String w = sc.next();      // next word
String line = sc.nextLine(); // rest of the line
```

In LogicQuest's problems the input is read for you, but you'll need this everywhere else.

exercises.prompt: The input is `6 7`. What does this print?
exercises.why: The two numbers 6 and 7 come from the input, so it prints 42.

exercises.prompt: Which Scanner method reads the next whole number?
exercises.why: `nextInt()` reads an int. `next()` reads a word as a String.

exercises.prompt: Read a name and greet it: input `Ana` → `Hello, Ana`.
exercises.why: Create a `Scanner` on `System.in`, then `next()` reads one word.

exercises.prompt: Arrange the lines to read two numbers and print their sum.
exercises.why: Create the Scanner before reading, and read before printing.

exercises.prompt: Read an integer `n` and print `n` squared.
exercises.code:
Scanner sc = new Scanner(System.in);
// read n and print n * n
exercises.why: `sc.nextInt()` then print `n * n`.

exercises.prompt: Read two numbers and print their sum. It prints `57` for input `5 7`. Fix it.
exercises.why: `+` on Strings joins them. Read numbers with `nextInt()` so `+` adds.

java.title: Conditions

exercises.prompt: What does this print?
exercises.why: The first true branch wins. 15 is divisible by both, so `both` prints and the rest is skipped.

exercises.prompt: Which condition is true when `age` is between 13 and 19, inclusive?
exercises.why: Both limits must hold, so use `&&`. Java doesn't allow the chained `13 <= age <= 19`.

exercises.prompt: What does this print?
exercises.why: `cond ? x : y` picks `x` when true, `y` when false. 4 > 9 is false.

exercises.prompt: Print `even` or `odd`.
exercises.why: `==` compares; `=` would assign and not compile here.

exercises.prompt: It should print `adult` for 18 and above. For 18 it prints `minor`.
exercises.why: "18 and above" includes 18, so the check is `>=`.

exercises.prompt: Read a number and print `big` if it is greater than 100, otherwise `small`.
exercises.why: Exactly 100 is not greater than 100, so it's `small`.

exercises.why: Starts at 0 and stops before 3: 0, 1, 2.

java.title: Arrays
java.intro:
An array holds a fixed number of values of one type:

```java
int[] nums = {4, 8, 15};
int[] zeros = new int[5];   // five zeros
nums[0]          // first element
nums.length      // 3, no brackets
```

exercises.prompt: What does this print?
exercises.why: Index 1 is the second element. After changing it to 100, 3 + 100 = 103.

exercises.prompt: What does this print?
exercises.why: `new int[4]` starts as four zeros; only index 2 changed.

exercises.prompt: For `int[] a = {5, 6, 7};`, which is the last element?
exercises.why: Indexes go 0..length − 1. `a[3]` throws ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException.

exercises.prompt: Find the largest value.
exercises.why: Walk the array and keep the biggest value seen so far.

exercises.prompt: Arrange the lines to print the sum of the array.
exercises.why: Create the array and the accumulator before the loop, print after it.

exercises.prompt: Read `n`, then `n` numbers. Print how many of them are negative.
exercises.why: Read with a loop into `a[i]`, then count with a second loop.

java.title: Methods (functions)
java.intro:
A method packs logic under a name. In LogicQuest problems you write `solve`:

```java
static int square(int x) {   // return type, name, parameters
    return x * x;
}
```

`static` lets `main` call it directly. `void` means it returns nothing.

exercises.prompt: What does this print?
exercises.why: twice(5) is 10, twice(1) is 2, so 12.

exercises.prompt: A method that only prints and gives nothing back has which return type?
exercises.why: `void` means no return value.

exercises.prompt: Complete the method that returns the larger of two ints.
exercises.why: The method gives back an int, and `return` sends the value out.

exercises.prompt: What does this print?
exercises.why: Each call runs the method body once with a different `name`.

exercises.prompt: `isEven(4)` should return true, but this doesn't compile. Fix the method.
exercises.why: Every path must return something. Java reports `missing return statement`.

exercises.prompt: Complete `cube` so it returns `n * n * n`. The program reads `n` and prints `cube(n)`.
exercises.why: Replace `return 0;` with the real calculation.

java.title: Reading errors
java.intro:
Errors are messages, not failures. Read the **first line** and the **line number**.

- **Compile errors** (before running): `';' expected`, `cannot find symbol` (typo or undeclared variable),
  `incompatible types` (wrong type).
- **Runtime exceptions** (while running): `ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException`, `ArithmeticException: / by zero`,
  `NullPointerException`.

exercises.prompt: `error: cannot find symbol  symbol: variable totl` most likely means…
options: You misspelled a variable name or didn't declare it
exercises.why: Java doesn't know `totl`. Usually a typo of `total`.

exercises.prompt: Which line throws `ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException`?
exercises.why: An array of 3 has indexes 0, 1, 2. Index 3 is outside.
exercises.code: int[] a = new int[3];

exercises.prompt: Fix the typo so it prints `30`.
exercises.why: `cannot find symbol: totl`. Match the name you declared.

exercises.prompt: This crashes with `/ by zero` when there are no items. Print `0` in that case instead.
exercises.why: Guard the division: check `count == 0` before dividing.

exercises.prompt: `incompatible types: String cannot be converted to int`. Fix it so it prints `8`.
exercises.why: Text isn't a number until you convert it: `Integer.parseInt(s)`.

exercises.prompt: Your loop prints one value too few. What's the most likely cause?
exercises.why: Off-by-one: check where the loop starts and whether the end should be included.

python.title: Hello, output
python.intro:
`print(x)` shows `x` and then moves to a new line. No semicolons, no `main` needed:
a Python file simply runs from top to bottom.

`print(a, b)` puts a space between the values. `print(x, end="")` stays on the same line.

exercises.prompt: What does this print?
exercises.code:
print("Hello")
print("World")
exercises.why: Each `print` ends with a newline, so the words land on two lines.

exercises.prompt: What does this print?
exercises.code:
print("Log", end="")
print("ic", end="")
print("Quest")
exercises.why: `end=""` replaces the newline with nothing, so the pieces join.

exercises.prompt: What does `print("a", "b", "c")` show?
exercises.why: Commas in `print` separate values with one space by default.

exercises.prompt: Print `1-2-3` using one print call.
exercises.code: print(1, 2, 3, sep=___)
exercises.why: `sep` sets what goes between the values (a space by default).

exercises.prompt: What does this print?
exercises.code:
print("2 + 3")
print(2 + 3)
exercises.why: Inside quotes it's text and printed as-is. Without quotes Python does the maths first.

exercises.prompt: This should print `Ready` but crashes. Fix it.
exercises.code: Print("Ready")
exercises.solution: print("Ready")
exercises.why: Python is case-sensitive. The error says `NameError: name 'Print' is not defined`.

python.title: Variables and types
python.intro:
A variable is a name pointing at a value. No type keyword is needed; Python works it out:

```python
age = 21          # int
price = 9.5       # float
name = "Yash"     # str
done = True       # bool (capital T)
```

`type(x)` tells you what you have.

exercises.prompt: What does this print?
exercises.code:
x = 10
x = x + 5
print(x)
exercises.why: `x = x + 5` reads 10, adds 5, and stores 15 back in `x`.

exercises.prompt: Which value is a `bool` in Python?
exercises.why: Booleans are `True` and `False`, capitalised. `"True"` in quotes is a string.

exercises.prompt: What does this print?
exercises.code:
first = "Logic"
second = "Quest"
print(first + second)
print(first, second)
exercises.why: `+` joins strings with no space; a comma in `print` adds one.

exercises.prompt: Swap `a` and `b` in one line.
exercises.code:
a = 1
b = 2
a, b = ___, ___
print(a, b)
exercises.why: Python evaluates the right side first, then assigns: a gets old b, b gets old a.

exercises.prompt: Arrange the lines so the program prints `20`.
exercises.why: A name must have a value before you use it.

exercises.prompt: This should print `Age: 21` but crashes with a TypeError. Fix it.
exercises.code:
age = 21
print("Age: " + age)
exercises.solution:
age = 21
print("Age: " + str(age))
exercises.why: You can't `+` a string and an int. Convert with `str(age)` (or use `print("Age:", age)`).

python.title: Operators
python.intro:
`/` always gives a float: `7 / 2` is `3.5`. Use `//` for whole-number division: `7 // 2` is `3`.
`%` is the remainder, `**` is power.

`x += 3` is short for `x = x + 3`. There is no `x++` in Python.

exercises.prompt: What does this print?
exercises.code:
print(7 / 2)
print(7 // 2)
print(7 % 2)
print(2 ** 5)

exercises.prompt: What does this print?
exercises.code:
x = 5
x += 3
x *= 2
x -= 1
print(x)

exercises.prompt: What is `2 + 3 * 4` in Python?
exercises.why: `*` happens before `+`: 3 × 4 = 12, then 2 + 12.

exercises.prompt: What does this print?
exercises.code:
print(-7 % 2)
print(-7 // 2)
exercises.why: Python's `//` rounds **down** (to -4) and `%` follows the sign of the right number (1). Java and JavaScript give -1 and -3.

exercises.prompt: Print the last digit of `n`, then `n` without its last digit.
exercises.code:
n = 1234
print(n ___ 10)
print(n ___ 10)
exercises.why: `% 10` gives the last digit; `// 10` removes it. `/ 10` would give 123.4.

exercises.prompt: This should print `5`, the number of full boxes of 4 you can fill from 22 eggs, but prints `5.5`.
exercises.code:
eggs = 22
print(eggs / 4)
exercises.solution:
eggs = 22
print(eggs // 4)
exercises.why: Full boxes is whole-number division: `//`.

python.title: Strings and characters
python.intro:
A `str` is text. A single character is just a string of length 1.

- `len(s)` → number of characters
- `s[i]` → character at index `i` (from 0); `s[-1]` is the last one
- `ord("a")` → 97, `chr(98)` → `"b"`
- Compare text with `==`.

exercises.prompt: What does this print?
exercises.code:
s = "quest"
print(len(s))
print(s[0])
print(s[-1])
exercises.why: Negative indexes count from the end: `s[-1]` is the last character.

exercises.prompt: What does this print?
exercises.code:
c = "a"
print(ord(c) + 1)
print(chr(ord(c) + 1))
exercises.why: `ord` turns a character into its code (97); `chr` turns a code back into a character.

exercises.prompt: Which expression is True when `s` is `"abc"`?
exercises.why: Indexes go 0..len − 1. `s[3]` raises IndexError and strings have no `.length`.

exercises.prompt: Print every character of `word` on its own line.
exercises.why: `range(len(word))` gives the indexes 0, 1, 2.

exercises.prompt: What does this print?
exercises.code:
s = "Hi"
s = s + "!"
print(s * 2)
exercises.why: `+` joins strings, and `* 2` repeats the string twice.

exercises.prompt: Read a word and print its first and last character separated by a space. For `logic` print `l c`.
exercises.code:
w = input()
# print first and last character
exercises.solution:
w = input()
print(w[0], w[-1])
exercises.why: First is `w[0]`, last is `w[-1]`.

python.title: Reading input
python.intro:
`input()` reads one line as a **string**. Convert it to use it as a number:

```python
n = int(input())                    # one number
a, b = map(int, input().split())    # two numbers on one line
```

In LogicQuest's problems the input is read for you, but you'll need this everywhere else.

exercises.prompt: The input is `6 7`. What does this print?
exercises.code:
a, b = map(int, input().split())
print(a * b)
exercises.why: The two numbers 6 and 7 come from the input, so it prints 42.

exercises.prompt: What type does `input()` return?
options: It depends on what you type
exercises.why: Always a string. `int(...)` converts it.

exercises.prompt: Read a name and greet it: input `Ana` → `Hello, Ana`.
exercises.code:
name = ___()
print("Hello, " + name)
exercises.why: `input()` reads the line the user typed.

exercises.prompt: Arrange the lines to read two numbers (one per line) and print their sum.
exercises.why: Read both numbers before adding.

exercises.prompt: Read an integer `n` and print `n` squared.
exercises.code: # read n and print n * n
exercises.solution:
n = int(input())
print(n * n)
exercises.why: `int(input())`, then print `n * n`.

exercises.prompt: Read two numbers and print their sum. It prints `57` for input `5 7`. Fix it.
exercises.code:
a, b = input().split()
print(a + b)
exercises.solution:
a, b = map(int, input().split())
print(a + b)
exercises.why: `split()` gives strings, and `+` joins strings. Convert with `map(int, ...)`.

python.title: Conditions

exercises.prompt: What does this print?
exercises.why: The first true branch wins. 15 is divisible by both.

exercises.prompt: Which condition is True when `age` is between 13 and 19, inclusive?
exercises.why: Python allows chained comparisons. `&&` is not Python syntax; use `and`.

exercises.prompt: What does this print?
exercises.code:
a, b = 4, 9
bigger = "a" if a > b else "b"
print(bigger)
exercises.why: `x if cond else y` picks `x` when the condition is true. 4 > 9 is false.

exercises.prompt: Print `even` or `odd`.
exercises.code:
n = 8
if n % 2 ___ 0:
    print("even")
___:
    print("odd")
exercises.why: `==` compares. `else:` needs its colon too.

exercises.prompt: It should print `adult` for 18 and above. For 18 it prints `minor`.
exercises.why: "18 and above" includes 18, so the check is `>=`.

exercises.prompt: Read a number and print `big` if it is greater than 100, otherwise `small`.
exercises.code:
n = int(input())
# your if / else here
exercises.why: Exactly 100 is not greater than 100, so it's `small`.

python.title: Loops
python.intro:
```python
for i in range(1, 6):     # 1, 2, 3, 4, 5  (stops BEFORE 6)
    print(i)

n = 10
while n > 0:
    n = n // 2
```

`range(5)` is 0..4, `range(a, b)` is a..b−1, `range(a, b, step)` jumps by step. `break` and `continue` work as usual.

exercises.prompt: What does this print?
What does this print?
exercises.code:
total = 0
for i in range(1, 5):
    total += i
print(total)
exercises.why: 1 + 2 + 3 + 4 = 10. The 5 is not included.

exercises.prompt: What does this print?
exercises.code:
n = 20
steps = 0
while n > 1:
    n = n // 2
    steps += 1
print(steps)
exercises.why: 20 → 10 → 5 → 2 → 1: four halvings.

exercises.prompt: Print 5, 4, 3, 2, 1 on separate lines.
exercises.code:
for i in range(5, ___, ___):
    print(i)
exercises.why: Count down with step −1. The stop value 0 is not included.

exercises.prompt: Arrange the lines to print only the odd numbers from 1 to 5.
exercises.why: `continue` skips the print for even numbers.

exercises.prompt: It should print 1 to 5 but stops at 4. Fix the loop.
exercises.code:
for i in range(1, 5):
    print(i)
exercises.solution:
for i in range(1, 6):
    print(i)
exercises.why: `range` stops before its end value. To include 5, the end must be 6.

python.title: Lists
python.intro:
A list holds values in order:

```python
nums = [4, 8, 15]
zeros = [0] * 5       # five zeros
nums[0]               # first
nums[-1]              # last
len(nums)             # 3
nums.append(16)       # add to the end
```

exercises.prompt: What does this print?
exercises.code:
a = [3, 6, 9]
print(len(a))
print(a[1])
a[1] = 100
print(a[0] + a[1])
exercises.why: Index 1 is the second element. After changing it, 3 + 100 = 103.

exercises.prompt: What does this print?
exercises.code:
a = [0] * 4
a[2] = 7
for x in a:
    print(x, end=" ")
print()
exercises.why: `[0] * 4` is four zeros; only index 2 changed.

exercises.prompt: For `a = [5, 6, 7]`, which expression raises IndexError?
exercises.why: Valid indexes are 0, 1, 2 (and −1, −2, −3). 3 is outside.

exercises.prompt: Find the largest value without using `max()`.
exercises.why: Walk the list and keep the biggest value seen so far.

exercises.prompt: Arrange the lines to print the sum of the list without `sum()`.
exercises.why: Create the list and the accumulator before the loop, print after it.

exercises.prompt: Read `n`, then a line of `n` numbers. Print how many of them are negative.
exercises.code:
n = int(input())
a = list(map(int, input().split()))
# count the negatives
exercises.solution:
n = int(input())
a = list(map(int, input().split()))
count = 0
for x in a:
    if x < 0:
        count += 1
print(count)
exercises.why: Loop over the list and add 1 for each value below zero.

python.title: Functions
python.intro:
```python
def square(x):
    return x * x

print(square(4))   # 16
```

A function without `return` gives back `None`. In LogicQuest problems you write `solve`.

exercises.prompt: What does this print?
exercises.code:
def twice(x):
    return x * 2

a = twice(5)
print(a + twice(1))
exercises.why: twice(5) is 10, twice(1) is 2, so 12.

exercises.prompt: What does this print?
exercises.code:
def shout(word):
    print(word + "!")

result = shout("hey")
print(result)
exercises.why: `shout` prints, but it doesn't return anything, so `result` is `None`.

exercises.prompt: Complete the function that returns the larger of two numbers.
exercises.code:
___ max2(a, b):
    if a > b:
        ___ a
    return b

print(max2(3, 8))
exercises.why: `def` starts a function; `return` sends the value back.

exercises.prompt: What does a Python function return if it has no `return` statement?

python.title: Reading errors
python.intro:
Python prints a **traceback**. Read the **last line** first: it names the error. The line above shows where.

- `NameError` → a name doesn't exist (typo, or used before defining)
- `TypeError` → wrong type for the operation (e.g. `"a" + 1`)
- `IndexError` → index outside the list or string
- `ZeroDivisionError`, `ValueError` (e.g. `int("abc")`)
- `IndentationError` → the spaces at the start of a line don't line up

exercises.prompt: `NameError: name 'totl' is not defined` most likely means…
options: A typo or a variable used before it was created
exercises.why: Python doesn't know `totl`; usually a typo of `total`.

exercises.prompt: Which line raises `IndexError`?
exercises.why: A list of 3 has indexes 0, 1, 2 (and −1..−3). 3 is outside.

exercises.prompt: Fix the typo so it prints `30`.

print(total)
exercises.solution:

total = total + 20
print(total)

javascript.title: Variables and types
javascript.intro:
Declare with `let` (can change) or `const` (can't be reassigned). Never use the old `var`.

```js
let age = 21;          // number
const price = 9.5;     // number too: JS has one number type
const name = "Yash";   // string
let done = true;       // boolean
```

`typeof x` tells you the type.

javascript.title: Operators
javascript.intro:
`/` always gives a decimal: `7 / 2` is `3.5`. For whole-number division use `Math.trunc(7 / 2)` (or `Math.floor` for non-negative numbers).
`%` is the remainder, `**` is power.

`x += 3` is short for `x = x + 3`, `x++` adds 1. Compare with `===` and `!==`; avoid `==`.

javascript.title: Strings and characters
javascript.intro:
A string is text. A single character is a string of length 1.

- `s.length` → number of characters (a property, no brackets)
- `s[i]` → character at index `i` (from 0); `s[s.length - 1]` is the last
- `s.charCodeAt(i)` → code number, `String.fromCharCode(98)` → `"b"`
- Compare text with `===`.

javascript.title: Reading input
javascript.intro:
Node reads everything the user typed (stdin) at once. Split it into lines, then convert:

```js
const lines = require("fs").readFileSync(0, "utf8").split("\n");
const n = Number(lines[0]);                       // one number
const [a, b] = lines[1].split(" ").map(Number);   // two numbers on one line
```

In LogicQuest's problems the input is read for you, but you'll need this everywhere else.

javascript.title: Reading errors
javascript.intro:
Node prints the error type and a stack trace. Read the **first line** and the `main.js:LINE` location.

- `ReferenceError: x is not defined` → typo, or used before declaring
- `TypeError: ... is not a function` / `Cannot read properties of undefined` → wrong value, often from a bad index
- `SyntaxError` → missing bracket, quote or comma
- Silent bugs: `undefined` and `NaN` in your output usually mean an index or conversion went wrong.

exercises.prompt: `ReferenceError: totl is not defined` most likely means…
options: A typo or a variable used before it was declared
exercises.why: JavaScript doesn't know `totl`; usually a typo of `total`.

exercises.prompt: Your output shows `NaN`. What's a likely cause?
options: Adding a number to `undefined` (e.g. reading past the end of an array)
exercises.why: `undefined + 1` is `NaN`. Check indexes and `Number(...)` conversions.

exercises.prompt: Your loop prints one value too few. What's the most likely cause?
exercises.why: Off-by-one: check where the loop starts and whether the end should be included.
